title: Strait Toll Plan Turns into Trade Talks the Next Day, but the Oil Market Has Not Settled Down
part1: As soon as the show began, the first idea to appear was: “Charge goods that pass through the strait.” Trump posted that the United States would seek 20% reimbursement from all cargo passing through, to cover the cost of keeping the Strait of Hormuz safe. But this was a proposal, not a fee already in effect. The fee system had not gone into action.
part2:
But the next day, the scene changed suddenly. Trump posted that he would replace the toll plan with trade and investment deals between Gulf countries and the United States. He said the decision was based on “very productive talks” with Middle Eastern leaders. The bill quickly turned into papers for trade talks. Quite a striking change of costume.

So, did oil prices also feel safe enough to bring the curtain down? The answer was not so simple. After the announcement, Brent futures briefly gave up some of their gains, but soon returned to a high level close to where they had been before the announcement. At the time of publication, they were up about 2.6%, above $85 a barrel.
part3:
What remained onstage was concern about supply. Concerns continued over attacks between the United States and Iran, a blockade at sea, and the safety of tankers. Even after the toll plan changed costumes, worries about the strait did not leave the stage.

The main topic changed from charges on cargo to trade and investment. But judging by market moves, worries about supply seemed to remain unchanged. Though the news was about a faraway strait, what mattered in the end was the movement in oil prices. A quick change in the story alone was not enough to bring the curtain down.
in_one_line: Trump replaced his proposed Strait of Hormuz toll with trade talks, but oil-market worries persisted.
